Electronic Components
LED vs LDR: Difference Between a Light Emitting Diode and a Light Dependent Resistor

An LED turns current into light, while an LDR turns light into a change of resistance. We compare both parts side by side, test them with a multimeter and wire them into one working night lamp circuit.

Comparison table Symbols and curves Multimeter tests Night lamp circuit Divider calculator

LED vs LDR is a classic exam and lab question, because the two parts look alike but work in opposite directions. We compare construction, symbols, curves, tests and one circuit that uses both.

Hello everyone, today we are going to compare LED vs LDR, the light source and the light sensor you meet in almost every electronics lab.
Quick Answer

What is the difference in LED vs LDR for light circuits?

LED vs LDR comes down to the direction of energy: an LED is a PN junction diode that emits light when forward current flows, while an LDR is a cadmium sulphide resistor whose resistance falls as light rises. A Kingbright L53LID red LED drops about 2.0 V at 20 mA, and a GL5528 LDR reads 10 to 20 kΩ at 10 lux.

PointLEDLDR
JobEmits light (output)Senses light (input)
PhysicsElectroluminescencePhotoconductivity
PolarityAnode and cathodeNone, either way round
Key ratingVF about 2.0 V at 20 mA (red)10 to 20 kΩ at 10 lux
SpeedNanoseconds20 to 30 ms

What Is the Difference Between LED and LDR?

The LED vs LDR difference is simple: an LED is an output device that makes light from current, and an LDR is an input device whose resistance changes with the light falling on it. One is a diode with polarity, the other is a resistor with none.

FeatureLEDLDR
Device typePN junction diodePhotoconductive resistor, no junction
PolarityLong lead is the anodeNon polar, works on AC too
Limits30 mA DC, 5 V reverse (L53LID)100 mW, 150 V (GL5528)
Typical useIndicators, lighting, optocouplersDusk switches, night lamps, alarms

For the full theory of each part, read our companion posts on how an LED works and the LDR working principle.

Do You Know?

In LED vs LDR physics, both parts depend on a semiconductor band gap. A red LED emits photons of about 2 eV, and a CdS cell responds best near 520 to 540 nm, close to where the eye is most sensitive.

Advertisement

How Is an LED Built and How Does It Make Light?

An LED is a small PN chip sitting in a reflector cup on the cathode lead, joined to the anode lead by a fine gold wire. When you forward bias it, electrons recombine with holes at the junction and each recombination releases a photon.

This is electroluminescence, and the band gap of the chip sets the colour, not the tint of the epoxy. The epoxy dome only shapes the beam, which the Kingbright L53LID datasheet quotes as a 60 degree viewing angle.

Photon energy E (eV) = 1240 ÷ λ (nm)
Red at 627 nm: 1240 ÷ 627 = 1.98 eV
So VF is about 2.0 V at 20 mA
Blue at 470 nm: 2.64 eV, VF near 3 V

This is why blue and white LEDs need more voltage than red ones. If junctions are new to you, our notes on what a semiconductor is and the main diode types fill in the background.

How Is an LDR Built and How Does It Sense Light?

An LDR, also called a photoresistor or photocell, is a zigzag track of cadmium sulphide laid between two comb shaped electrodes on a ceramic disc. Light frees electrons in the CdS, so the track conducts better and the resistance falls.

There is no junction, so current flows either way and there is no anode or cathode. The long, narrow zigzag path keeps the dark resistance high, so the change with light is large.

R = R10 × (10 ÷ lux)γ
GL5528: R10 = 15 kΩ, γ = 0.7
At 100 lux: 15 × 0.10.7 = 3.0 kΩ
At 1 lux: 75 kΩ

Gamma is the slope of the line on log scales, and GL5528 datasheets give 0.6 to 0.7. Take 15 kΩ, the middle of the 10 to 20 kΩ band, as R10 and trim on the bench.

Quick Tip

Wait at least 10 seconds after covering an LDR before reading its dark resistance. The Advanced Photonix datasheet measures it after 10 seconds.

LED vs LDR Symbol, Polarity and Characteristic Curves

In LED vs LDR symbols, the LED is a diode triangle and bar with two arrows pointing out, and the LDR is a resistor box with two arrows pointing in, often inside a circle. The curves follow the same logic: LED current against voltage, LDR resistance against light.

The LED curve stays flat to about 1.6 V and then rises steeply, so a small voltage change gives a big current change. That is why you drive an LED through a series resistor, as our LED resistor calculation guide shows, never from a bare voltage.

The LDR line is nearly straight on log scales, from about 75 kΩ at 1 lux to 3 kΩ at 100 lux. It tells day from night well but measures lux poorly.

Where an LDR does well
  • Cheap, robust, two leads and no polarity
  • Huge change, from 1 MΩ dark to a few kΩ in room light
  • Spectral peak near the human eye
Where an LDR falls short
  • Slow, and up to a second to recover in the dark
  • Wide tolerance, so each circuit needs trimming
  • Cadmium is restricted in Europe under RoHS

How to Test LED and LDR With a Multimeter

For the LED vs LDR test, put the LED in diode mode and the LDR in resistance mode. A good LED conducts one way only, while a good LDR reads the same both ways but changes strongly when shaded.

1
Identify the part
An LED has a longer anode lead and a flat on the cathode side. An LDR shows a wavy track on its face.
2
LED in diode mode
Red probe on the long lead. A red LED reads 1.6 to 2.0 V and may glow.
3
Reverse the probes
Expect OL. Low both ways means a shorted LED.
4
LDR in ohms mode
Use the 2 MΩ range. Room light gives a few kΩ.
5
Shade the LDR
Cover it for 10 seconds. It should climb to hundreds of kΩ.

Many meters cannot light a blue or white LED in diode mode, so OL on those colours does not prove a fault. Try 5 V through a 330 Ω resistor instead.

LED vs LDR field tip
If an LDR reading keeps creeping up for several seconds after you cover it, the part is fine. CdS cells recover slowly, so the drift is normal and not a loose probe.
SymptomLikely causeWhat to check
LED reads OL both waysOpen LED, or meter too weak for blue or whiteRetry with 5 V and 330 Ω
LED reads low both waysShorted LED, often after running with no resistorReplace and add a resistor
LDR stuck at OL in lightCracked track or broken leadReplace the cell

LED and LDR Circuit: How Does an Automatic Night Lamp Work?

A night lamp shows the LED vs LDR roles clearly: the LDR senses, the LED is the load and a BC547 NPN transistor switches. In daylight the LDR pulls the base low, and in darkness its resistance rises, the base voltage rises and the LED turns on.

R1 and the LDR form a voltage divider on the base, and the transistor starts to conduct at about 0.6 V. Our post on the basics of transistors explains how that small base current controls a larger collector current.

With R1 at 22 kΩ, the base reaches 0.6 V when the LDR falls to about 3 kΩ, which for a GL5528 is close to 100 lux. Below that light level the lamp turns on.

Switch point: RLDR = 22 × 0.6 ÷ 4.4 = 3.0 kΩ (about 100 lux)
Dark base current: (5 minus 0.7) ÷ 22 kΩ = 0.195 mA
LED current: (5 minus 2.0 minus 0.2) ÷ 150 Ω = 18.7 mA
At 50 lux: RLDR = 4.86 kΩ, base node 0.90 V, lamp on

With a BC547B gain of 200 or more, 0.195 mA of base current allows far more than 18.7 mA, so the transistor saturates. Ohm’s law gives that 18.7 mA, and it stays under the 30 mA limit of the L53LID.

LDR Divider and Night Lamp Switch Calculator
LDR resistance, base node voltage and lamp state
LDR 4.86 kΩ, base node 0.90 V, transistor ON, lamp lit

The calculator treats the divider as unloaded, so in a real circuit the base clamps near 0.6 to 0.7 V once the transistor conducts. If you move the LDR to the top, use a voltage divider calculator.

Do You Know?

An LED can also act as a weak light sensor, because its junction produces a small voltage when light falls on it. It is much less sensitive than a real photodiode.

Advertisement

Where Are LED and LDR Used in Instrumentation?

In LED vs LDR applications, LEDs serve as indicators, light sources and opto isolator inputs, while LDRs serve as slow, cheap light sensors. Plants use far more LEDs, because fast light sensing has moved to photodiodes.

Street lights
Dusk to dawn switches use an LDR to turn lamps on at night.
Opto isolation
The LED inside an optocoupler drives a phototransistor across a barrier.
Light beam alarms
Breaking the beam raises the LDR resistance and trips the alarm.

The optocoupler working principle is the clearest case of an LED used as a signal source. On conveyors, the photoelectric sensors in automation pair an LED emitter with a fast receiver, not an LDR.

Myth: An LDR is just an LED used backwards.
Fact: An LDR is a CdS resistor with no PN junction.
Myth: An LDR is fast enough to count pulses.
Fact: A GL5528 needs 20 ms to rise and 30 ms to fall, so faster jobs need a photodiode.
Myth: An LED can go straight across a 5 V supply.
Fact: Without a series resistor the current shoots past the 30 mA rating and the LED fails.
Quick Tip

If your night lamp flickers at dusk, check whether the LED light reaches the LDR. Shield the sensor, or add hysteresis with a comparator.

Which Light Sensor Should You Choose Instead of an LDR?

Choose an LDR for slow, low cost switching, a photodiode for fast or accurate measurement, and a phototransistor for more signal at moderate speed. In an LED vs LDR pairing, the LED only supplies the light.

LDR (CdS cell)

Resistance falls with light, logarithmic, tens of ms.

Best for: Dusk switches, night lamps
Slow
Photodiode

Current proportional to light, fast and linear.

Best for: Lux meters, encoders, data links
Fast
Phototransistor

Photodiode with built in gain, microsecond speed.

Best for: Slot sensors, counters
Gain

Our comparison of photodiode and phototransistor covers speed and gain in detail. For an accurate light reading, a photodiode with a transimpedance amplifier is the standard front end.

  • Only day or night switching? An LDR is enough.
  • Need response faster than about 50 ms? Use a photodiode.
  • Selling in Europe? Check RoHS status before using CdS.
  • Driving an LED? Size the resistor for 20 mA or less.

LED vs LDR FAQ

What is the main difference between LED and LDR with example?

In LED vs LDR terms, an LED emits light when forward current flows, while an LDR changes resistance with light. A red LED drops about 2.0 V at 20 mA, and a GL5528 LDR reads 10 to 20 kΩ at 10 lux.

How to calculate LDR resistance at a given lux step by step?

Use R = R10 × (10 ÷ lux) raised to gamma, where R10 is the resistance at 10 lux. For a GL5528 with R10 of 15 kΩ and gamma 0.7, at 100 lux you get 15 × 0.2 = 3.0 kΩ.

How do you check an LED and an LDR with a multimeter?

Check the LED in diode mode with the red probe on the long lead, and expect about 1.6 to 2.0 V for red and OL when reversed.

A good LDR on the 2 MΩ range reads a few kΩ in room light and hundreds of kΩ when covered.

Why does my LDR night lamp flicker or stay on in daylight?

Flicker usually means the LED light reaches the LDR, or the light sits right at the switch point with no hysteresis. A lamp that stays on in daylight often has an open LDR, which leaves the base pulled high by R1.

Which is better for fast light sensing, LDR or photodiode?

A photodiode is far better, because it responds in microseconds or less while a GL5528 LDR needs 20 ms to rise and 30 ms to fall. Choose an LDR only for slow jobs such as day and night switching, and use a photodiode for pulse counting.

What We Learn Today

  • The LED vs LDR difference is one of direction, because an LED turns forward current into light while an LDR turns light into resistance.
  • Test an LED in diode mode with the red probe on the long lead, and test an LDR on a high ohms range while shading it.
  • An LDR and resistor divider driving a BC547 transistor make a simple night lamp that lights a red LED below about 100 lux.
